item.title: Sisters strike back: have women finally had enough of the caring burden?
item.description: When elderly parents need looking after, it’s usually their daughters who do the bulk of the work – as highlighted by a viral Saturday Night Live skit. Here, siblings share how to spread the load more evenly When Simran and her older brother were growing up, he was always the golden boy. He brought home A* grades and basked in their parents’ praise, while she was the rebel, scolded for bunking off school. So it’s ironic, she says, that in middle age she became the dutiful daughter, giving up a career she loved to care for their ailing parents while her brother lives what seems to her a remarkably carefree life overseas. “It’s funny how the tables have turned,” she says. “The person they spoiled is the person who has never been there for them, never even bought my mum and dad a birthday card. I had dreams and ambitions of things I wanted to do, but I can’t pursue them now.” Continue reading...

item.title: The picture-perfect California beach where visitors keep dying
item.description: The deaths of four people and the disappearance of another in six months have raised questions about Panther beach and what can be done to keep people safer Panther state beach in California looks like something out of a dream: it lies among the coastal coves between Santa Cruz and Half Moon Bay, open directly to the Pacific. Dramatic shale cliffs climb 50ft into the air, while tiny pocket beaches sit between them, pummeled by large waves. In this wild-seeming place, young people flock to escape city life: take pictures, build fires, and have colorful adventures that drip from postcards and Instagram carousels. Continue reading...

item.title: A riot grrrl song inspired me to leave a controlling relationship
item.description: My jealous guitarist boyfriend stopped me from pursuing my own musical dreams, but then a powerful anthem by Sleater-Kinney gave my situation a soundtrack One winter afternoon in Maine in the mid-1990s, a stranger slipped a love note into my messenger bag. I was in my first year of high school. I played jazz clarinet, dabbled in teen-witch tarot reading, and spent hours reading Virginia Woolf. He was a picture of alternative rock intrigue: lanky with shoulder-length dark hair, pale skin and an ever-present band T-shirt. We had never talked before. I was elated he chose me. A gregarious but socially awkward nerd, I had yearned for a boyfriend, but even the “alternative” boys at our high school usually went for the long-legged lacrosse girls. I felt plucked from obscurity and delivered into something important and adult. Continue reading...

item.description: What the former UAE ambassador has done and said so far is alarming those, like me, who have witnessed the slaughter of our people When war broke out in Sudan in April 2023 , I went to New York to ask members of the UN security council to help stop the atrocities. item.title: ‘I thought I could outsmart biology’: more and more women are freezing their eggs – but what happens next?
item.description: The procedure has never been more popular, with high-profile women such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez publicly getting in on the act. But outcomes vary. Women around the world tell their stories Earlier this year, US congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made an announcement that many interpreted as a sign of a future presidential run. It had nothing to do with policies or elections. Instead, she was freezing her eggs , a process she documented with a series of intimate social media posts. From a medical perspective, oocyte cryopreservation (more commonly known as egg freezing) is a lengthy and often expensive procedure. It begins with a slate of scans and blood tests, followed by a course of self-injected hormones to stimulate the ovaries. After 10 to 14 days, patients undergo surgery to extract their available eggs. item.title: Georgina Hayden’s recipe for fennel, clementine and chilli Christmas porchetta
item.description: This rolled pork joint makes a worthy centrepiece for when you’re feeding a crowd While I’m a sucker for tradition, I don’t ever fully embrace turkey at Christmas. Sure, it can be nice, but ultimately it’s just not my favourite meat. And if I’m going to all the effort of making the most delicious side dishes, then I want them accompanying something I love. If that needs to be poultry, then you’re more likely to find me roasting a capon, but if anything goes, then I turn to pork. Whether it’s a slow-cooked shoulder, a glazed ham or even basic pork belly, I love it. And this porchetta is such a straightforward and worthy centrepiece. It’s laced with flavour, can be prepared in advance and retains its heat for a long time. So, if oven space is limited, as it so often is at Christmas, leave it resting on the side, loosely covered, and it will be happy. Continue reading...

item.title: Young country diary: Now I know that chalk streams are very, very cool | Polly
item.description: Hertfordshire: I’m amazed by how clear and icy (and shallow) the water is, and if I’m lucky I’ll see a brown trout in the gravel We have been learning about ecosystems at school, so I decided to go down to my local chalk stream, part of the River Mimram , in search of wild brown trout and learn about their environment. Chalk streams are incredibly rare , with only about 200 in the entire world! They are famous for being crystal clear because the water is filtered through underground chalk rocks. It really was so pure-looking that I could see every single pebble gleaming on the riverbed. I was keen to kick off my shoes to get a closer look, especially because the water looked super refreshing on a warm autumn afternoon, although it was still shallow after the hot summer. item.title: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
item.description: A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebook It often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more! Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

item.title: Brit-splaining Botham and the impossible task of defining a sporting life without limits | Will Woodward
item.description: Explaining the England all-rounder and now great-grandfather reveals a career that refuses to fit in a single box Across the Guardian sportsdesk this week it emerged that a young American colleague didn’t know who Ian Botham was. And why should she? She is young and American. And so the rest of us Brit-splained in five sentences, rehearsed here – and edited to make us sound better than we actually did. Botham is comfortably among the top five most famous living British sportspeople, certainly among those of a certain age. In 1981 he won (almost) single‑handed (arguably) the greatest Ashes series by bending it to his will. He was on the front pages as well as back in the 1980s, for soft drugs, suspensions and shagging. He is a member of the House of Lords. He is the most English of sports stars, Australians love him, and his grandson James plays rugby union for Wales, which is why we started talking about him. item.title: The radical clarity of NAZA makes You Can See Everything seem irrelevant | Charlotte Higgins
item.description: When I was reporting on the arts in the 2000s, the view was ‘politics be damned’. But in times of war and catastrophe, cinema becomes committed – as it should In 2004, I was weeks into my new job as the Guardian’s arts correspondent when I was sent off to cover the Cannes film festival for the first time. The opening movie was Wolfgang Petersen’s Troy . Desperate for a news line, I stuck up my hand in the packed press conference, and – nerdy ex-classics student that I was – asked Brad Pitt if there were any analogies to be drawn between the continuing Iraq war and the mythical Trojan war. It was not a crazy question. Art uses myth to reflect on contemporary horrors all the time. The parallels between Homer and the war in the Middle East seemed obvious. A western alliance invaded an eastern nation on a shaky pretext. The killing of thousands had followed – and, at times, a shameful abuse of the defeated. Pitt duly answered gracefully. Continue reading...

item.title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst

I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there . Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. item.title: Walking the Wirral Way: winter birdwatching and coastal history on the Dee estuary
item.description: Once a hive of maritime activity, the estuary is now a haven for wildlife – but you don’t have to be a birder to appreciate its tousled beauty Cheshire’s Hadlow Road is a fine railway station. A redbrick building with a cream signal box and a spick-and-span platform, it has neat benches, potted flowers, and a cafe that serves a restorative flat white. But the metal billboards fixed to the brickwork – advertising, among other things, Lever’s Cattle Cakes and Hudson’s Super Soap – are evidence of what really makes the station notable: the last train came through in 1962. “Nearly 65 years ago,” confirms the man repainting the signal box. I sip my coffee and stare along the line. Plenty has changed in this corner of the country since Hadlow Road’s heyday. The rural station is now a preserved heritage attraction, but for almost 100 years it was a stop on a branch line of the Birkenhead Railway. We all have our pros and cons It’s been fun, from a mental health perspective, to hear the government advise the country to Be Ready, stockpiling supplies for an unspecified catastrophe that could happen at any time. What can we realistically do about targeted tech outages, power loss and Russian cyber-attacks? On my last big shop, I half-heartedly doubled up the items, while remaining unconvinced 30 Lindt balls and two bags of Chilli Heatwave Doritos are going to help much when the fireball comes. I’m anxious but lazy, so my doomsday prepping mostly amounts to watching TV that fuels my paranoia. item.title: The Guide #271: The strange success of You Can See Everything gives me hope for the future of risk-taking creatives
item.description: In this week’s newsletter: Former magician Nathan Fielder pulls some stunning tricks in this docu-drama, proving audiences love a world of weirdness Warning: while this article is spoiler-free for You Can See Everything, it contains spoilers for The Curse I don’t think we knew what to do with You Can See Everything. The documentary drama – in which comedian turned millennial auteur Nathan Fielder is granted unlimited access to disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes – premiered just over a month ago in the US, and only a week ago in the UK. And yet we have already entirely devoured it, dissecting it to death. Our appetite for analysis has been so ferocious that there is almost nothing left to say about the text itself: questions such as, “Was Holmes lying?”, “Was she manipulated?” and “Was Fielder compromised as a film-maker?” have already been discussed ad nauseam. item.title: ‘Who asked that? You should be ashamed of yourself!’: Judi Dench answers questions from Ian McKellen, Lorraine Kelly, David Hare and more
item.description: Fans and famous friends put their nosiest questions to the 91-year-old actor It’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. It’s one of the smallest rooms in her Elizabethan home: timber beams, terracotta-painted walls, her father’s consulting-room desk and chair within touching distance, together with the bronze “Dr Dench” plaque that used to hang on the railings outside their family home in York. Behind Judi’s head hangs an enormous painting of her as M, presented as a gift on her last day of filming on Skyfall . Through the latticed windows is a view on to the garden, which is crowded with trees she plants for lost friends and family – a beloved oak, a tribute to her late husband, actor Michael Williams, towers above the pond. Even though the room is suffused with autumn sunshine, all the lights are on in the house. Judi has always needed light around her – she’s been afraid of the dark since she was small. item.title: Watching Wild Horse Nine in Santiago brings Pinochet’s tyranny back to dreadful life
item.description: Having lived through the real life horror it was chilling to see Martin McDonagh’s film so close to its historical site. Would its audience hear the urgent message? It was chilling for me, as a survivor of the 1973 coup that installed a bloody 17-year dictatorship in Chile, to watch Wild Horse Nine at a theatre in Santiago, a viewing haunted by those who had been killed and disappeared during the reign of General Augusto Pinochet. Though Martin McDonagh’s film is set shortly before the military takeover, it disturbingly foretells the atrocities that are to come, a terrifying future that is known to the protagonists, Chris and Lee, because, as CIA agents, they have been instrumental in the conspiracy to destroy the peaceful revolution of democratically elected president Salvador Allende. Continue reading...

item.title: Tom yum party mix, chicory boats and peanut sprout skewers: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for Christmas canapés
item.description: A Christmas party mix of moreishy savoury, spicy, salty and citrussy bites to suit every palate. Just add a glass or three of fizz Party food should be about maximum pleasure and minimum fuss. It should feel generous, delicious, easy to eat, and simple enough to put together, not least so the host can enjoy the festivities, too. ’Tis the season for crunchy, salty snacks such as my dangerously addictive tom yum party mix that can be scarfed by the fistful, a refreshing citrus salad piled up on the best edible vessel, namely chicory, and sprouts on sticks with peanut sauce that can be passed around. Importantly, all of these leave one hand free for a glass of something deliciously festive. Happy Christmas everyone! Continue reading...

This was the first competitive game for Emma Hayes’ team since their Olympic gold medal match in August 2024, the end of two years of only friendlies. Given the global advances in women’s soccer over the years, maybe El Salvador could spring an all-time upset. The suspense ultimately lasted for eight minutes and 20 seconds. item.description: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law. It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. item.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
item.description: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any hum

item.title: The Guardian view on the Children’s Booker prize: everyone is a winner | Editorial
item.description: In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked “Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize , as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote. The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity. item.title: ‘Genuinely emotional’: the world-conquering Chicken Shop Date’s final, eye-opening episode
item.description: After a 12-year run, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s last episode of Chicken Shop Date – a therapy session with Esther Perel – is being shown in cinemas. It’s a fittingly grand finale for a YouTube cult favourite that far outgrew its medium The decision to screen the full final series of Chicken Shop Date in cinemas before the finale airs on YouTube is, it could be argued, overkill. The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say. And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop. item.title: Ross County have 102 goals and British football’s best start but is it a fairytale?
item.description: There is cynicism and jealousy but one of County’s top scorers is 39 as club try to climb leagues again after tumbling It was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Ross County 1 Cove Rangers 1 (Keir 52). Would Cove, scrapping for survival in Scottish League One, put an unlikely end last Saturday to the most emphatic run in British senior football? Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. item.description: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns. The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.” Continue reading...

item.description: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. item.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
item.description: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

item.title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
item.description: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. item.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
item.description: The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered. Continue reading...

item.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days

item.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
item.description: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

item.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
item.description: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, four months before the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to victory at the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentinos Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

item.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
item.description: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

item.title: Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03813-6 The number of recorded cases of the mosquito-borne disease worldwide rose by a factor of 34 over 34 years.

item.title: The Mona Lisa Lottery
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03521-1 Worth the wait.

item.title: The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03809-2 Generic versions of an effective HIV drug have been approved, and an HIV vaccine is on the horizon. Now is no time for funders to take their foot off the pedal.

item.title: A guide to the Nature Index
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5 A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

item.title: Succumbing to certainty is a failure in science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03837-y Researchers can face pressure from policymakers and politicians to provide single, definitive answers to complex challenges. They should resist, says Andy Stirling.

item.title: Rare gene variants can affect a person’s height by up to 17 centimetres
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03872-9 An analysis of 1.4 million people uncovered rare gene variants that are helping to unpick the genetic architecture behind the heritability of height.

item.title: Enzymatic reactions adapted to make ‘living’ chains of sugars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03382-8 By tuning the binding between enzymes that chain sugars together and the molecules that initiate the reaction, precise chain lengths have been made for biological studies.

item.title: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0 Awe, anxiety and opportunity: mathematics community shares mixed emotions following the solution of the field’s biggest unsolved problem.

item.title: Just eight universities dominate Nobel and other top economics prizes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03333-3 Economics is the outlier — top prizes in science, engineering and other social sciences go to researchers at a greater variety of institutions.

item.title: An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 Reconstruction of radiative forcing resulting from worldwide peatland drainage over the past two centuries reveals a persistent net warming effect caused by the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions over that of avoided CH4 emissions.

item.title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11275-z A multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human coronary artery disease provides a framework for mapping disease-associated genetic variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

item.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 Architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer drive cell state diversification through mechanochemical reprogramming of stem cell identities.

item.title: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

item.title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11353-2 Quantum confocal microscopy enables deterministic preparation of high-photon-number Fock-like states with up to 500 photons, reducing photon-number variance by 21.5 dB and achieving record displacement-sensing precision 19.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit.

item.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11287-9 RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) is enhanced by redesigned TnsA and a holo complex whose coordinated conformational licensing reveals a conserved mechanistic framework for engineering highly active CASTs.

item.title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11341-6 Dental morphology and proteomic analyses of fossils from southern China identify lineages with and without Denisovan affinity, indicating the diversity of hominin populations in this region in the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

item.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5 Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.

item.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11146-7 Integrated photonics could overcome key size, power and performance trade-offs in augmented-reality glasses, enabling compact, efficient displays while opening opportunities across quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

item.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11309-6 Coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas are demonstrated in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains, providing a foundation for topologically protected qubits in longer chains.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11196-x Structural analyses reveal the mechanism underlying RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) and provide a framework for developing CASTs into site-specific genome-editing tools.

item.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11231-x This Review covers the current state of research into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) from a variety of perspectives, focusing on the clinical context.

item.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11151-w The use of an extremophile fungus-derived gene decouples the trade-off of drought stress and reduced crop yield by boosting drought resilience and increasing yields in wheat, rice and maize.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

item.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

item.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

item.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

item.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

item.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
item.description: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
item.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

item.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

item.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

item.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
item.description: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

item.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. item.description: The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. Continue reading...

item.title: Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge
item.description: Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more Mail us with all of your questions and answers “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?” The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. item.description: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
